title: How do soft plants stand up without wood?
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: How does a plant stay upright?
How do you make limp lettuce crisp again?

explain.say: A tree stands up with wood, but a lettuce or a sunflower seedling has no wood at all. It is held up by water pressure inside its cells, called turgor.

draw.text: How do soft plants stand up without wood?

explain.say: Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: a plant cell. Look at the cell wall, the cell membrane and the vacuole. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.

draw.text: How do soft plants stand up without wood?

explain.say: Each cell has a big vacuole full of watery sap. Water flows in by osmosis and the vacuole swells, pushing outward against the stiff cell wall, like air pumped into a bike tyre.
Millions of firm, pumped-up cells press against each other, making stems and leaves stiff enough to hold up their own weight against gravity.
When the soil dries out, water leaves the cells faster than it arrives. The vacuoles shrink, the pressure drops, and weight wins: the plant wilts. Water it, and within hours it stands up again.

faq.a: Plants wilt when they lose water faster than their roots can take it in. Their cells go floppy as the pressure inside drops, so stems and leaves droop under their own weight.
Turgor is the pressure of water inside a plant cell pushing out against the cell wall. It keeps soft plant parts firm, the way air keeps a balloon or tyre firm.
asks: How does water hold a plant up?

faq.q: Why does crisp lettuce go limp?
faq.a: Picked lettuce keeps losing water but can no longer drink, so its cells lose turgor and go limp. Soaking it in cold water lets the cells take water back in and crisp up again.
asks: How do you make limp vegetables crisp?

faq.a: Trees have wood, made of cells with thick walls stiffened by a tough substance called lignin. Wood stays strong even without water pressure, which is why trees do not wilt like seedlings.
Usually yes, if you water it before its cells are damaged. Water flows back into the cells, turgor returns and the plant stands up again, often within a few hours.
asks: Will my droopy plant come back?

facts: Turgor pressure inside plant cells can be higher than the air pressure in a car tyre.
Wood gets its strength from lignin, which stiffens the walls of its cells.
Wilting is the sign that a plant is losing water faster than it can take it in.

quiz.say: What holds up a soft, non-woody plant?
quiz.show: What holds up a soft, non-woody plant?
quiz.why: Full vacuoles push against the cell walls, making every cell firm.

wrong.1: Air spaces in leaves are for gases, not support.
wrong.2: Plants have no bones at all.
